claim: More time and information yield better decisions is widely accepted.
source: It is widely accepted that more time and information yield better decisions.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus in the introduction.

claim: Some decisions are extremely fast and yet accurate.
source: However, some decisions manage to be extremely fast and yet accurate.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by examples provided throughout the manuscript.

claim: Highspeed decisions use simplifying heuristics that work well for common conditions but lack flexibility.
source: The trick of such highspeed decisions appears to be the use of simplifying heuristics that works well for the most common condition but lacks flexibility otherwise.
evidence: This is presented as a prevailing view in the field that the study challenges.

claim: Archerfish make highspeed decisions faster than an Olympic sprinter can respond to the start gun.
source: In this decision, archerfish observe the initial speed, direction, and height of falling prey and then use these initial values to turn right towards where ballistically falling prey would later land. To analyze the limits in flexibility of this highspeed decision, we developed and critically tested a system that allowed us to replace the usual ballistic relation between initial prey motion and the expected landing point with another deterministic rule.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Adult archerfish can reprogram their highspeed decision to a new rule.
source: We discovered that, surprisingly, adult fish could reprogram their highspeed decision to the new rule.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: After reprogramming, fish can immediately generalize their decision to novel untrained settings.
source: Moreover, after reprogramming their decision fish were immediately able to generalize their decision to novel untrained settings, showing a remarkable degree of abstraction in how the decision circuit represented the novel rule.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The decision circuit can simultaneously use two distinct sets of rules, one for each of two visually distinct objects.
source: The decision circuit is even capable of simultaneously using two distinct sets of rules, one for each of two visually distinct objects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The archerfish decision lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff and is made in less than 100 ms.
source: The flexibility and level of cognition are unexpected for a decision that lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff and is made in less than 100 ms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4J, K and cited literature (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008).

claim: The quality of decisions depends on how much time and effort is devoted to them.
source: It is common wisdom that the quality of our decisions depends on how much time and effort we devote to them.
evidence: This is stated as common knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The expected trade-off between the speed of a decision and its accuracy is well documented across many species from slime mold to primates.
source: The expected trade-off between the speed of a decision and its accuracy is very well documented not only in humans but for many decisions across many species from slime mold to primates (Chittka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chittka et al., 2009.

claim: A class of very rapid decisions deviates from the speed-accuracy tradeoff rule.
source: A class of very rapid decisions appears, however, to deviate from this rule (e.g. VanRullen and Thorpe, 2001; Romo and Salinas, 2001; Uchida et al., 2006; Stanford et al., 2010; Stanford and Salinas, 2021; Gladwell, 2005; Gigerenzer, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In rapid decisions, accuracy does not increase when more time is available.
source: In these decisions, accuracy does not increase when more time is available.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of rapid decisions and supported by examples.

claim: Rats can reliably categorize odors based on just one sniff (about 300 ms), and more sampling time leads to no further improvement.
source: For example, rats can reliably categorize odors based on just one sniff (about 300 ms), and more sampling time leads to no further improvement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Uchida et al., 2006; Uchida and Mainen, 2003; Zariwala et al., 2013.

claim: The absence of speed-accuracy tradeoff in rats holds equally for both simple and complex odor-discrimination tasks.
source: This is not due to the simplicity of the task and holds equally for both simple and complex odor-discrimination tasks (Uchida et al., 2006; Uchida and Mainen, 2003; Zariwala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Archerfish monitor the speed, direction, and height of falling prey and rapidly turn towards the corresponding ballistic impact point.
source: Archerfish, the subject, of the present study, monitor the speed, direction, and height of falling prey and rapidly turn towards the corresponding ballistic impact point (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Rossel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In archerfish decisions, no relation was found between the average response latency and the accuracy of the turns.
source: In this decision, no relation was found between the average response latency and the accuracy of the turns (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlegel and Schuster, 2008.

claim: Humans can reliably classify natural visual images after surprisingly brief glimpses of only 20–40 ms.
source: Humans can reliably classify natural visual images after surprisingly brief glimpses (of only 20–40 ms, see VanRullen and Thorpe, 2001; Bacon-Macé et al., 2005; Uka and DeAngelis, 2003; Harwerth et al., 2003; De Bruyn and Orban, 1988; Snowden and Braddick, 1991; Nachmias, 1967; Tulunay-Keesey and Jones, 1976)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The perceptual parts of human decision making can often be much faster than previously thought.
source: and more recent approaches demonstrated that the perceptual parts of human decision making can often be much faster than previously thought (Stanford and Salinas, 2021; Salinas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Hitters in baseball have only 400 ms to move their bat to the optimal strike point, a movement that can only be based on about 70 ms of visual processing.
source: For example, hitters in baseball have only 400 ms to move their bat to the optimal strike point, a movement that can only be based on about 70 ms of visual processing (Higuchi et al., 2016; Gray and Cañal-Bruland, 2018; Kidokoro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Some slow and complex human decisions can deviate from the expected speed-accuracy tradeoff and be superior when made with lesser time and lesser information.
source: Finally, even slow, and probably complex human decisions, such as which product to buy in a store, can sometimes deviate from the expected speed-accuracy tradeoff and be superior when made with lesser time and lesser information (Gladwell, 2005; Gigerenzer, 2007; Dudey and Todd, 2001; Beilock et al., 2004; Gigerenzer and Brighton, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Most decisions show speed-accuracy trade-offs.
source: Despite these deviations, there is of course no doubt that most decisions do show speed-accuracy trade-offs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Decisions that lack a speed-accuracy trade-off manage to be fast because they profit from using simplifying heuristics.
source: One reason could be that the decisions that lack a speed-accuracy trade-off manage to be so fast because they profit from using simplifying heuristics (Gladwell, 2005; Gigerenzer, 2007).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Simplifying heuristics allow being fast and accurate for specific conditions but lack flexibility under more variable conditions.
source: As we illustrate with a specific example below this allows being fast and accurate for specific conditions that enormously reduce the complexity of the problem. The decisions would, however, not be useful under more variable conditions as they lack the flexibility to adjust to these other conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hoverfly example and general reasoning.

claim: Flexibility to cope with changing conditions could distinguish slower decisions from highspeed decisions.
source: In other words, the flexibility to cope with changing conditions could be what distinguishes the more common slower decisions (i.e. those with speed-accuracy tradeoffs) and the more unusual highspeed decisions.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis.

claim: Evidence from baseball outfielders, frisbee-catching dogs, and hoverfly chases supports the view that highspeed decisions lack flexibility.
source: The evidence that is presently available – from the movement of baseball outfielders and frisbee-catching dogs (McBeath et al., 1995; Shaffer et al., 2004) to the chase of hoverflies (Collett and Land, 1978) – seems to support this view (also see Gladwell, 2005; Gigerenzer, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Male hoverflies use a rapid open-loop strategy to intercept passing females based on hardwired assumptions about speed, size, and acceleration.
source: An elegant series of experiments showed that this very rapid and accurate decision is based on hardwired assumptions about the speed v and size (and hence detection distance D) of a typical female hoverfly and about the typical maximum rate a of the male's acceleration. These variables appear all to be genetically imprinted in the neural circuits that govern the male turn decision.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Collett and Land, 1978 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Challenging male hoverflies with objects that deviate from their hardwired assumptions causes them to make robust errors predicted by a simple heuristic model.
source: Expectedly, challenging the males with objects that deviated from these assumptions, caused them to make robust errors that were predicted based on a simple heuristic model that the fly appears to use (Collett and Land, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Collett and Land, 1978.

claim: The turn decisions of male hoverflies are an example of a very fast and accurate decision that lacks flexibility but has evolved to work for a restricted set of conditions.
source: The turn decisions of male hoverflies are thus an excellent example of a very fast and accurate decision that lacks flexibility but has evolved to work specifically for a restricted set of conditions. This is all that is ever required in the specific behavioral context (Collett and Land, 1978).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Archerfish down aerial prey with shots of water and use an open-loop strategy to arrive simultaneously with their prey at the water surface.
source: Archerfish down aerial prey with shots of water and also use an open-loop strategy to arrive simultaneously with their prey as soon as it hits the water surface.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Archerfish sample visual information on the speed, height, and direction of the initial falling motion and turn towards where ballistically falling prey would later land.
source: The responding fish, shooters, and bystanders alike, sample visual information on the speed, height, and direction of the initial falling motion and turn right towards where ballistically falling prey would later land.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Archerfish turns are part of a maneuver called C-start.
source: These turns are part of a maneuver called C-start (Schuster, 2023; Wöhl and Schuster, 2007), that also lends the fish the level of speed that, when kept, make it arrive just in time.
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Fully accurate turns in archerfish can be initiated in as little as 40 ms depending on visual contrast, water temperature, height of prey, and distance from the future landing point.
source: Depending on visual contrast, water temperature, height of prey, and the distance from the future landing point, fully accurate turns can be initiated in as little as 40 ms (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlegel and Schuster, 2008 and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: In contrast to male hoverflies, ecological constraints in archerfish do not allow similar simplifying assumptions.
source: In contrast to the conditions in the male hoverfly, the ecological constraints in archerfish do not allow similar simplifying assumptions and archerfish can respond appropriately from a large range of distances and initial orientation and when encountering targets of unusual size or speed (as will be shown below).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B, with supporting data to be shown later.

claim: Archerfish shoot down aerial prey with jets of water.
source: This decision is an essential part of the hunting behavior of archerfish, in which the fish shoot down aerial prey with jets of water (Dill, 1977; Schuster, 2018; Gerullis and Schuster, 2014; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Once prey is dislodged, archerfish have only the little time remaining until prey hits the water surface to turn and dash off to be at the impact point just when prey arrives.
source: Once a prey insect is successfully dislodged, shooters and bystander archerfish have only the little time that remains till prey hits the water surface to turn and dash off to be at the impact point of prey just when it arrives there.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the hunting behavior.

claim: In the wild, missing the impact point or not being there in time would typically mean losing prey to more numerous competing surface-feeding fish.
source: In the wild, missing this point or not being there in time, would typically mean losing prey to the more numerous competing other surface-feeding fish (Rischawy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rischawy et al., 2015.

claim: Archerfish watch the initial movement of dislodged prey and then quickly and accurately select the appropriate turn and take-off to be at the later landing point at the right time.
source: The solution archerfish have evolved to secure their prey and to outperform their competitors is to watch the initial movement of dislodged prey and then quickly and accurately select the appropriate turn and take-off to be at the later landing point at the right time (e.g., Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Rossel et al., 2002; Schuster, 2023; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Archerfish predictive C-starts are among the fastest C-starts known in fish.
source: Their so-called predictive C-start decisions are among the fastest C-starts known in fish and are initiated much faster than an Olympic sprinter can respond to the start gun (Sillar et al., 2016; see Video 1 for an appreciation of the decision's speed).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sillar et al., 2016 and Video 1.

claim: When archerfish were challenged with prey that was prevented from falling but only slid on a glass plate, they still responded with turns toward the appropriate virtual ballistic impact points.
source: When many such interspersed rare cases with sliding flies were later analyzed, it turned out that fish still responded, although nothing fell. Moreover, their response latency – measured between the onset of prey motion and the onset of the turns – was the same as in most tests in which real prey was falling (Rossel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rossel et al., 2002 and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: For each set of conditions with sliding flies, the fish turned to the appropriate virtual impact point calculated based on ballistics.
source: This analysis revealed that for each set of conditions the fish had turned to the appropriate virtual impact point, calculated based on ballistics, just as they would toward a real later impact point of real falling prey (Rossel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rossel et al., 2002 and illustrated in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The archerfish decision circuit maps the initial values of motion to the turn angle needed to reach the ballistic landing point.
source: This implies that the fish were able to map the initial values of motion to the turn angle they needed to produce and that this mapping is appropriate for ballistically falling objects (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Archerfish turn decisions exclusively use information sampled during a brief interval after onset of prey motion.
source: The archerfish's turn decisions exclusively use information that is sampled during a brief interval after onset of prey motion (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Reinel and Schuster, 2014; Reinel and Schuster, 2018a; Reinel and Schuster, 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The information used in archerfish turn decisions includes the initial height from which prey is falling.
source: This information even includes the initial height from which prey is falling (Reinel and Schuster, 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinel and Schuster, 2018a.

claim: All experiments have shown that the archerfish start decision does not use or has no access to prior information.
source: In other words, all experiments available have shown that the start decision does not use or has no access to prior information. Instead, it relies exclusively on information sampled once prey starts moving.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous experimental findings.

claim: All archerfish studied in the lab and in the wild consistently showed robust turn decisions towards the inferred ballistic landing points.
source: Because all archerfish studied so far in the lab and in the wild consistently showed robust turn decisions towards the inferred ballistic landing points (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Rossel et al., 2002; Rischawy et al., 2015; Reinel and Schuster, 2014; Reinel and Schuster, 2018a; Reinel and Schuster, 2018b; Wöhl and Schuster, 2006; Wöhl and Schuster, 2007), we expected the decision to be hardwired to ballistics.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hardwiring the decision circuit to ballistic falling patterns could be fixed genetically and/or established during the early ontogeny of the fish.
source: Hardwiring the decision circuit to ballistic falling patterns could be fixed genetically and/or established during the early ontogeny of the fish.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis.

claim: An initial aim to the ballistic landing point would be in error for non-ballistically falling prey, but this initial error could be corrected during the actual approach trajectory.
source: While an initial aim to the ballistic landing point would be in error for non-ballistically falling prey, this initial error of the fish's turn could always be corrected during the actual approach trajectory.
evidence: This is a logical inference about potential alternative strategies.

claim: Adult archerfish are capable of learning to extract and use a novel non-ballistic rule of how to connect the three independent input variables of prey motion to the point to which they must turn to receive a reward.
source: Nevertheless, we demonstrate here that the decision is not hardwired to ballistic falling. We show that adult archerfish are capable of learning to extract and to use a novel non-ballistic rule of how to connect the three independent input variables of prey motion to the point to which they must turn to receive a reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: A virtual reality system was developed that presents information with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution as needed by the decision circuit.
source: To be useful for the question at hand, the system needs to fulfill four conditions: (i) First, it must present the information with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution as needed by the decision circuit.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement and demonstrated in the Results section.

claim: The VR system presents the reward at the positions and times as required by ballistic or arbitrary other rules without adding further information that could interfere with the decision.
source: (ii) Second, it needs to present the reward at the positions and times as required by ballistic or arbitrary other rules but without adding further information that could interfere with the decision.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement and demonstrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The VR system works so well that there is no statistically detectable difference between virtual and real responses.
source: (iii) Third, the VR system would have to work so well that there is no statistically detectable difference between virtual and real responses.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement and demonstrated in Figure 3C-G.

claim: The VR system keeps the fish motivated for many months of experimentation during which the fish exclusively face virtual objects.
source: (iv) Finally, the system must keep the fish motivated for the many months of experimentation during which the fish will exclusively be facing virtual objects.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement and implicitly demonstrated by the long-term training data.

claim: The successful VR setup used an LCD screen at a frame rate of 120 frames per second and employed custom-made automatic feeders.
source: After several unsuccessful attempts – including LED-based arrangements used in earlier work (Strauss et al., 1997; Schuster et al., 2002; Reiser and Dickinson, 2008) – we found a system that completely fulfilled all four crucial conditions. In the following, we present evidence for that successful system (Figure 3). The setup worked, surprisingly, with an LCD screen at a frame rate of 120 frames per second and employed custom-made automatic feeders that were non-transparent and provided food at the right time and place, coupled to the motion shown on the screen.
evidence: This is described in the Methods and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The VR setup readily and continuously elicited turns toward the calculated ballistic impact point.
source: First, the setup readily and continuously elicited turns toward the calculated ballistic impact point (Figure 3B–G).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B-G.

claim: Operating the feeders without showing motion on the screen failed to elicit turn decisions.
source: Operating the feeders without showing motion on the screen failed to elicit turn decisions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When feeders were placed systematically offset from the ballistic virtual impact points, turns were aimed at the VIPs and not at the feeders.
source: Most importantly, when feeders were placed not at the ballistic virtual impact points (VIPs) but systematically offset from them, then turns were aimed at the VIPs and not at the feeders – even though this was where the fish got their reward (Figure 3B; 15° offset, n=353; 30° offset, n=198).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: The decisions were only based on the movement information presented on the screen and were not influenced by cues from the feeders or from any other landmarks in the tank.
source: In other words, even in the presence of the feeders were the decisions only based on the movement information that was presented on the screen and were not influenced by cues from the feeders or from any other landmarks in the tank.
evidence: This is an inference from the data in Figure 3B.

claim: No aspect of the decisions was statistically different under real and virtual conditions.
source: Given the limitations in the temporal resolution of the screen it is striking that no aspect of the decisions was statistically different under real and virtual conditions (Figure 3C–G, n=101 (real) and n=85 (virtual) starts).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C-G.

claim: The accuracy of the aim was not statistically different between real and virtual conditions (p=0.506).
source: The accuracy of the aim achieved at the end of the turns (measured as introduced in Figure 2) was not statistically different (p=0.506, Mann-Whitney; Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3C.

claim: Turns always minimized the error to the impact point, regardless of whether it was real or virtual.
source: and always minimized the error to the impact point, regardless of whether it was real or virtual (difference from zero: p=0.903 (real), p=0.455 (virtual); One-Sample Signed Rank)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no significant difference in variance between real and virtual conditions (p=0.589).
source: with also no significant difference in variance (p=0.589, Brown-Forsythe).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3C.

claim: The turns had the same latency between real and virtual conditions (p=0.297).
source: The turns also had the same latency (between onset of prey motion and onset of the turns; p=0.297; Mann-Whitney; Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3D.

claim: There was no difference in bending duration under real and VR conditions (p=0.071).
source: and kinematics (Figure 3E: no difference in bending duration under real and VR conditions, p=0.071, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3E.

claim: Responses came from a large range of orientations and distances and were equally accurate across all distances and turn sizes.
source: Furthermore, responses came from a large range of orientations and distances and, most importantly, were equally accurate across all distances (Figure 3F) and turn sizes (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: The turn decisions were equivalent in all examined aspects (accuracy, latency, kinematics) to those obtained with real falling objects.
source: In summary, despite the limited frame rate of the screens and despite the need to use highly conspicuous feeders in the majority of the (rewarded) presentations, the turn decisions were equivalent in all examined aspects (accuracy, latency, kinematics) to those obtained with real falling objects.
evidence: This is a summary of the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: A new rule was introduced that generates a systematic and substantial deviation (of 14.9 cm) between the new VIPs and the ballistic VIPs.
source: Figure 4A introduces the new rule that we chose to face the fish with. It generates a systematic and substantial deviation (of 14.9 cm) between the new VIPs and the ballistic VIPs as inferred from the initial movement.
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: After the new rule was introduced, the movement direction is deflected by 39.8° to the left after the fish's typical decision time.
source: After having traveled straight throughout what was the previous decision time, the movement direction is deflected by 39.8° (to the left, s. Methods), and the reward is now presented at the appropriate 'deflected' VIP.
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: According to the new rule, the connection between initial movement and the point of reward is still precisely defined.
source: According to this new rule, the connection between initial movement and the point of reward is still precisely defined.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the new rule.

claim: Learning to turn according to the new rule requires the fish to learn non-trivial corrections that depend sensitively on the position of the responding fish.
source: It would require the fish to learn non-trivial corrections that can be appreciated by considering Figure 4B: Relative to the turn they had previously made for a given input constellation they would need to add a correction that is not constant but depends sensitively on the position of the responding fish.
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: A new map of corrections is required for every combination of input variables.
source: This map of corrections is, furthermore, not the same for all input constellations. Instead, a new map of the kind shown in Figure 4B is required for every combination of input variables (as illustrated with a simple example in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fish never ceased to respond with their characteristic turns during training to the new rule.
source: Interestingly, the fish never ceased to respond with their characteristic turns (response probability remained constant across all training blocks, p>0.08, Pairwise Chi-square).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the training data.

claim: The kinematics of the turns and latency remained constant during training to the new rule.
source: The kinematics of the turns and latency also remained constant (bending and straightening phase of their C-starts both p>0.28, latency p>0.07; Kruskal-Wallis).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the training data.

claim: The aims were systematically in error for the initial training blocks.
source: Furthermore, their aims were systematically in error for the initial training blocks (deviation from zero error to the deflected VIPs p≤0.001, One-Sample Signed Rank) as expected (Figure 4D; deviation of aim to ballistic VIPs from zero error p>0.06; One-Sample Signed Rank; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 4D and Video 3.

claim: After more than 1750 presentations (55 experimental days), the turns clearly minimized the error to the appropriate new 'deflected' VIPs and no longer to the ballistic ones.
source: However, gradually the errors made to the new 'deflected' VIPs became smaller and, after more than 1750 presentations (55 experimental days), the turns clearly minimized the error to the appropriate new 'deflected' VIPs (Figure 4C, E, F; Video 4) and no longer to the ballistic ones.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C, E, F and Video 4.

claim: In interspersed tests with only the initial linear part of motion shown, the errors made were not different from those made when the full trajectories were visible.
source: The errors made in the interspersed tests (n=68) were not different from those made when the full trajectories were visible (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: In interspersed tests with only initial movement shown and direction offset from feeder positions, the turns were still aimed at the new deflected VIPs.
source: Yet, the turns the fish made in these tests were still aimed at the new deflected VIPs (differences from zero error p=0.721 at 15° (n=197) and p=0.113 at 72° (n=145); One-Sample t-tests) but not at the feeders and also not at the ballistic VIPs (Kruskal-Wallis: p≤0.001 at 15°; p=0.005 at 72°; Dunn's p<0.05 for comparison of errors; Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 4G and Video 5.

claim: The turns made when only the linear initial motion was visible and when the VIPs were spatially offset from the feeders did not differ in latency or kinematics from the turns made without offset and with the full trajectory visible.
source: Furthermore, the turns – made when only the linear initial motion was visible and when the VIPs were spatially offset from the feeders – did not differ in latency (p=0.686, Kruskal-Wallis) nor in kinematics (bending duration: p=0.242, Kruskal-Wallis) from the turns made without offset and with the full trajectory visible (n=240).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data related to Figure 4G.

claim: The new turns were possible and equally accurate across a range of distances and turn angles.
source: Finally, the new turns were not restricted to just a few positions and orientations of the responding fish. Rather, they were possible and equally accurate across a range of distances and turn angles (Figure 4H, I).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4H and 4I.

claim: There was no significant linear or Spearman correlation between error magnitude and response latency in the re-programmed decisions.
source: For both plots, there was no significant linear (p=0.318, R2=0.005, Figure 4J; p=0.469, R2=0.004, Figure 4K) or Spearman correlation (p=0.128 and 0.174, respectively, in Figure 4J, K).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 4J and 4K.

claim: A highspeed decision that lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff can be flexibly reprogrammed to a new rule.
source: Our findings, therefore, demonstrate that a highspeed decision that lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff can be flexibly reprogrammed to a new rule.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: All training to the new rule was carried out exclusively with targets presented at only one height level.
source: This can be examined conveniently because all training to the new rule was carried out exclusively with targets presented at only one height level.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental design feature.

claim: Possible target speed levels were limited, and prey was of only one size during training.
source: In addition, possible target speed levels were limited, and prey was of only one size.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental design feature.

claim: The turns already minimized the error to the VIPs that were appropriate for the untrained novel height levels right from the start with no trend that errors would decrease.
source: Interestingly, the turns already minimized the error to the VIPs that were appropriate for the untrained novel height levels. They were appropriate right from start with no trend that errors would decrease (linear regression: all p>0.1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The turns minimized the error to the deflected landing point also at the untrained height levels.
source: A detailed analysis of the errors (Figure 5D, E) showed that the turns minimized the error to the deflected landing point also at the untrained height levels (difference from zero: both p>0.07; One-Sample t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: The turns were not directed to the ballistic landing point (prediction 'ballistic') at untrained height levels.
source: They were also not directed to the ballistic landing point (prediction 'ballistic;' both p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: The turns were not directed towards the deflected landing point at the training height (prediction 'substitute') at untrained height levels.
source: and not towards the deflected landing point at the training height (prediction 'substitute;' both p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: None of the characteristics of the turns had changed in the novel situation compared to those after training.
source: Again, none of the characteristics of the turns had changed in the novel situation compared to those after training (also n=30 right before these tests): latency: p=0.098, kinematics: p=0.177 (Kruskal-Wallis), variance of errors: p=0.188 (Brown-Forsythe).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing data before and after the height change.

claim: The new rule is not represented by updating a simple lookup table but in a way that allows immediate generalization to new untrained height levels.
source: In other words, the new rule is not represented by updating a simple lookup table but in a way that allows immediate generalization to the new untrained height levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the generalization data in Figure 5.

claim: When faced with a new absolute prey size, the trained fish immediately turned to the deflected landing points.
source: Again, the trained fish immediately turned to the deflected landing points (differences from zero error: each p>0.4, One-Sample Signed Rank; difference in aim before and after size change p=0.764, Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5F.

claim: Learning did not involve simplifying a priori assumptions about absolute prey size.
source: Hence, learning did also not involve simplifying a priori assumptions about absolute prey size.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 5F.

claim: When tests with lower than training speed were interspersed, the first 30 turns made at the lower speed minimized the error to the actual deflected VIP.
source: When tests with lower than training speed were interspersed among presentations with the speed levels as during training, then already the first 30 turns made at the lower speed (Figure 5G) minimized the error to the actual deflected VIP (difference from zero p=0.102; One-Sample t-test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5G.

claim: At untrained speed levels, turns did not minimize error to VIPs given by ballistics or by using predictions for the deflected VIPs based on the trained speed levels.
source: but not to the VIPs given by either ballistics (prediction 'ballistic;' p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank) or by using predictions for the deflected VIPs that are based on the trained speed levels (p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5G.

claim: Changing target size and speed did not affect the nature of the turns (latency, bending duration, variance of errors).
source: Comparing latency, bending duration, and the variance of errors (speed: last 30 presentations with only training speed; size: last 30 presentations with target size during training) showed that changing target size and speed also did not affect the nature of the turns. Latency and bending duration were not significantly different in the changed versus training conditions (at novel untrained speed: Latency: p=0.280, Mann-Whitney; Stage 1: p=0.076, Mann-Whitney. At novel untrained size: Latency: p=0.305, t-test; Stage 1: p=0.997, Mann-Whitney). Variance was even slightly reduced (and not increased) at the untrained target speed (p=0.021, Brown-Forsythe) and remained unchanged after the increase in target size (p=0.742, Brown-Forsythe).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: All tests show that the decisions had been reprogrammed in much more clever ways than predicted, allowing immediate generalization.
source: In summary, all tests show that the decisions had been reprogrammed in much more clever ways than predicted. Rather than independently changing the size of an unrewarding turn for each individual constellation – as would seem required because the input variables themselves are varied independently from each other – learning allowed immediate generalization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the generalization data in Figure 5.

claim: When trained fish were randomly shown two differently shaped objects (disk and triangle), the turns made in response to the 'ballistic object' initially still minimized the error to the deflected VIP.
source: However, in experiments to test this prediction, the turns made in response to the 'ballistic object' (rewarded at the ballistic VIP) initially still minimized the error to the deflected VIP (difference from zero error p=0.256; One-Sample Signed Rank; same variance as for disk p=0.343; Brown-Forsythe; first 160 responses to ballistic object) and not to the ballistic VIP point (difference to ballistic landing point: p=0.038, Mann-Whitney; Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: After 500 additional starts in response to the ballistic objects, turns were equally in error to the deflected and the ballistic VIPs.
source: However, after 500 additional starts in response to the ballistic objects, turns were equally in error to the deflected and the ballistic VIPs (p=0.648, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6B.

claim: The turns made to the moving disks remained unaffected throughout the same period and remained perfectly matched to the deflected landing point.
source: In contrast, the turns made to the moving disks remained unaffected throughout the same period and remained perfectly matched to the deflected landing point (difference from zero error p=0.273; One-Sample Signed Rank; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6C.

claim: After about 300 additional encounters of moving triangles, the turns minimized the error to the ballistic impact point when a triangle was shown.
source: After about 300 additional encounters of moving triangles the turns minimized the error to the ballistic impact point when a triangle was shown (error to ballistic VIPs p=0.836, error to deflected VIPs p=0.020; One-Sample Signed Rank; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6B.

claim: The turns continued to minimize the error to the deflected impact point whenever the disk was shown.
source: However, the turns continued to minimize the error to the deflected impact point whenever the disk was shown (error to ballistic p≤0.001, error to deflected p=0.084, n=187; One-Sample Signed Rank; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6C.

claim: In interspersed tests with only the initial straight paths shown for both disk and triangle, the turns were toward the ballistic landing point when the triangle was shown and to the deflected landing point when the disk was shown.
source: Again, the turns were toward the ballistic landing point when the triangle was shown (difference from ballistic p=0.075, from deflected p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank) and to the deflected landing point when the disk was shown (difference from ballistic p=0.008, from deflected p=0.412; One-Sample Signed Rank) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6D.

claim: Latency and kinematics of the turns were the same in the responses to triangles and disks.
source: Also, latency (p=0.189, Mann-Whitney; Figure 6E) and kinematics of the turns (bending duration; p=0.984; Mann-Whitney; Figure 6F) were the same in the responses to triangles and disks.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: Object shape determined which rule the decision used to determine the appropriate turn given the input data.
source: In other words, the nature of the turn decision was the same, but object shape determined which rule the decision used to determine the appropriate turn given the input data.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6D-F.

claim: All three individual fish that contributed most of the starts minimized the error to the appropriate VIP.
source: Our analysis showed that all three of the three individual fish that had contributed most of the starts in Figure 6 minimized the error to the appropriate VIP (Figure 6G; difference from zero error always p>0.1; One-Sample Signed Rank).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6G.

claim: The variability of the errors in applying the two rules did not differ in any of the individuals.
source: Also, the variability of the errors in applying the two rules did also not differ in any of the individuals (p=0.966; Brown-Forsythe).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6G.

claim: The decision circuit used by archerfish has the potential of simultaneously operating on two different rules.
source: This shows clearly that the decision circuit used by archerfish does have the potential of simultaneously operating on two different rules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6.

claim: In tests where the prey object revealed its shape only at motion onset, the decisions remained appropriate to the ballistic or deflected VIPs.
source: Under these conditions, the decisions remained appropriate to the ballistic (triangle; n=109 starts) or deflected (disk; n=46 starts) VIPs (difference from zero error to appropriate VIP: p=0.451 (triangle) and p=0.671 (disk); p≤0.001 for the alternatives, all One-Sample Signed Rank).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 7.

claim: The distribution of errors was not statistically different when shape cue was available 2 s prior versus only during the decision phase.
source: Furthermore, also the distribution of errors was not statistically different from those obtained with the shape cue available 2 s prior to the decision (p=0.269; Brown-Forsythe).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 7.

claim: The information needed to select which rule is to be used can be extracted in the very brief interval after motion onset, together with all other decision-relevant information.
source: Hence the information that is needed to select which rule is to be used can also be extracted in the very brief interval after motion onset, together with all other decision-relevant information.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 7.

claim: It is not required to instruct the decision circuit before target movement starts.
source: It is not required to instruct the decision circuit before target movement starts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 7.

claim: The study demonstrates that highspeed decisions that lack a speed-accuracy tradeoff do not necessarily lack flexibility.
source: Using the rapid turn decisions of hunting archerfish as an example we demonstrate that highspeed decisions that demonstrably lack a speed-accuracy tradeoff (Figure 4J, K, Schlegel and Schuster, 2008), do not necessarily lack flexibility.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The decision is not hardwired to ballistic falling patterns.
source: Using a virtual reality system that exploits key properties of this decision (Figures 2, 3) we were able to show that the decision is not hardwired to ballistic falling patterns.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: After a training phase with a new rule, the fish were able to rapidly turn towards the new points appropriate for their starting position and the combination of initial motion variables.
source: After a training phase in which the connection between initial motion and the point of reward had been systematically changed – according to a new rule – the fish were able to rapidly turn towards the new points, that were appropriate for their starting position and the combination of initial motion variables.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Generalization tests after reprogramming showed that the decision could immediately handle new constellations never encountered during the re-training phase.
source: Generalization tests after this reprogramming showed, furthermore, that the decision could immediately handle new constellations never encountered during the re-training phase
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The decision was capable of simultaneously handling two distinctly different rules, one for each of two visually different prey objects.
source: and that it was capable of simultaneously handling two distinctly different rules, one for each of two visually different prey objects.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The findings provide a striking counterexample to the view that highspeed decision making is generally based on simplifying heuristics and lacks flexibility.
source: Our findings provide a striking counterexample to the view that highspeed decision making is generally based on simplifying heuristics and lacks flexibility.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: None of the cognitive aspects described in the study is unique and not found in much slower behaviors.
source: None of the cognitive aspects we describe here is in any way unique and not found in much slower behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Archerfish generalize efficiently when they learn how to engage moving targets and to judge the absolute size of prey.
source: For example, archerfish generalize efficiently when they learn how to engage moving targets and to judge the absolute size of prey (Schuster et al., 2004; Schuster et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Recognizing and assigning a value to different visual shapes has been demonstrated in archerfish.
source: Also, recognizing and assigning a value to different visual shapes has been demonstrated much earlier (e.g. Rischawy and Schuster, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Many cognitive aspects have been described across the animal kingdom, including animals with far smaller brains.
source: and many aspects have been described across the animal kingdom, including animals with far smaller brains (Chittka and Niven, 2009; Chittka and Jensen, 2011; Giurfa, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: What is surprising is to find cognitive features in a decision made at reflex-like speed (less than 100 ms) that lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff.
source: What is surprising, therefore, is clearly not to find cognitive features in archerfish, but rather to find such features in a decision that is made at a very different timescale at reflex-like speed (less than 100 ms) and that lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff (Figure 4J, K; Schlegel and Schuster, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the key surprising finding.

claim: The complexity involved in reprogramming the archerfish highspeed decision is comparable to tasks considered highly sophisticated in many laboratory animals.
source: The complexity involved in reprogramming the archerfish highspeed decision must also not shy a comparison with tasks that are considered highly sophisticated in many laboratory animals (e.g., Asaad et al., 1998; Bunge, 2004; Fusi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The task the decision circuit of archerfish can handle in as little as 40 milliseconds is to conditionally switch between two complete rules of how to connect a three-dimensional set of input data to a continuum of possible motor outputs.
source: In comparison, the task the decision circuit of archerfish can handle in as little as just 40 milliseconds (see Figure 4) is not only to conditionally switch between two motor outputs but to switch between two complete rules of how to connect a three-dimensional set of input data to a continuum of possible motor outputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison to other sophisticated tasks.

claim: The plausible assumption that reflex speed implies reduced complexity and flexibility could have a similar foundation as the assertion that smaller brains have reduced cognitive capacities.
source: The plausible assumption that reflex speed implies reduced complexity and flexibility (Fusi et al., 2007; Wang, 2008) could have a similar foundation as the assertion that smaller brains have reduced cognitive capacities.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Substantial progress has been made on the assertion that smaller brains have reduced cognitive capacities, resulting in an impressive list of sophisticated cognitive features found in animals with bird- and fish brains.
source: Substantial progress has been made on this latter assertion, resulting in an impressive and continuously growing list of sophisticated cognitive features that were found in animals with bird- and fish brains (Bshary et al., 2002; Shettleworth, 2010; Güntürkün and Bugnyar, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Insect brains that operate with a millionth of the neurons of a human brain can handle a wide range of cognitive tasks.
source: Most impressively, it has been demonstrated that insect brains that operate with a millionth of the neurons of a human brain can handle a wide range of cognitive tasks (Chittka and Niven, 2009; Chittka and Jensen, 2011; Giurfa, 2013; Giurfa et al., 2001; Avarguès-Weber et al., 2012; Chittka, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Insect cognitive tasks include social or observational learning.
source: that even include social or observational learning (Chittka, 2017; Loukola et al., 2017; Bridges et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Learning can lead to the reprogramming of innate and supposedly hardwired behaviors in insects.
source: Of particular interest in our context is that it has even been demonstrated that learning can lead to the reprogramming of innate and supposedly hardwired behaviors in insects (Roussel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The reflex speed of some decisions made by animals with much larger brains will likely limit the size of the underlying neuronal circuitry, allowing only a subset of the brain to be used, a subset that could be considered a 'functional minibrain.'
source: The reflex speed of some decisions made by animals with much larger brains also will likely limit the size of the underlying neuronal circuitry, allowing only a subset of the brain to be used, a subset that could be considered a 'functional minibrain,'
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: The assertion that everything that is as fast as a reflex must be simple might suffer the same fate as the assertion that brains with fewer neurons must be simple.
source: The assertion that everything that is as fast as a reflex must be simple might, therefore, suffer the same fate as the assertion that brains with fewer neurons must be simple.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: The kinematics of archerfish turn decisions is completely equivalent to the C-starts that the fish produce to escape.
source: In the turn decisions of archerfish, specifically, it is known that the kinematics of their turn decisions is completely equivalent to the so-called C-starts that the fish produce to escape (Wöhl and Schuster, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Both the turn decisions (predictive C-starts) and the archerfish escape C-starts are among the fastest C-starts known in fish.
source: Both the turn decisions (also called predictive C-starts; Schuster, 2023) and the archerfish escape C-starts are among the fastest C-start known in fish (Wöhl and Schuster, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: At least the motor circuits of archerfish turn decisions are restricted to the well-known powerful hindbrain circuits of a comparably small number of tractable neurons, organized around the giant Mauthner neuron.
source: and so at least the motor circuits are restricted to the well-known powerful hindbrain circuits of a comparably small number of tractable numbers of neurons, organized around the giant Mauthner neuron (Korn and Faber, 2005; Machnik et al., 2018a; Machnik et al., 2018b; Hecker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The Mauthner neuron's rapidly conducting axon would be suited to initiate the turn but the recruitment of other hindbrain neurons is needed to account for the precision and adjusted straightening speed of the fish.
source: Its rapidly conducting axon would be suited to initiate the turn but the recruitment of other hindbrain neurons is needed to account for the precision and adjusted straightening speed of the fish (Wöhl and Schuster, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: To show that the decision has the potential to be reprogrammed requires careful experiments and controls, but one fish that can do it illustrates what the circuitry can do in principle.
source: To show that the decision has the potential to be reprogrammed – and that it can even operate on two rules – requires careful experiments and controls, but clearly one fish that can do it illustrates what the circuitry can do in principle.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a justification for the approach.

claim: The study analyzed a group of six fish that reached homogeneous stages of performances.
source: Here, we analyzed a group of six fish that reached homogeneous stages of performances.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: There could be large differences in the learning speed of the individuals.
source: Clearly, there could be large differences in the learning speed of the individuals.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility in the Discussion.

claim: An extremely exciting possibility is if the reprogramming would allow for some form of observational or even social learning.
source: An extremely exciting possibility – that we cannot presently address – is if the reprogramming even would allow for some form of observational or even social learning.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion.

claim: Rapid and precise turn decisions are required in archerfish because of the severe competition they often face.
source: We do believe, although the number of individuals that we were able to train and test in the present long endeavor is limited, that our findings are of relevance in the wild. First, rapid and precise turn decisions are required because of the severe competition archerfish often face.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting reasoning.

claim: Other surface-feeding fish are more numerous in Thailand and better equipped with mechanosensors and capable of using vision to guide pre-impact turns.
source: Other surface-feeding fish are not only more numerous in Thailand – and, therefore, likely to be closer at the landing point of the archerfish's prey – but they are better equipped with mechanosensors and are also capable of using vision to guide pre-impact turns.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: It is crucial for archerfish to outperform competitors by using fast and precise turn decisions.
source: It is, therefore, crucial for archerfish to outperform them by using fast and precise turn decisions (Rischawy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The clearly demonstrated capacity of archerfish decisions for being flexible has evolved because of competition and scarcity of aerial prey in many natural habitats.
source: We suggest that the clearly demonstrated capacity of these decisions for being flexible has evolved because of this competition and because of the scarcity of aerial prey at least in many natural habitats.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: Small prey will typically fall ballistically.
source: While small prey will typically fall ballistically (Rossel et al., 2002; Reinel and Schuster, 2018a),
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Larger prey will face considerable frictional forces and will not fall equally far.
source: larger prey will face considerable frictional forces and – all other conditions being equal – will, therefore, not fall equally far.
evidence: This is stated as a physical inference.

claim: Simply using hardwired circuitry for ballistically falling prey would produce wrong initial turns for larger items and would require subsequent corrections that cost precious time.
source: Simply using hardwired circuitry for ballistically falling prey would produce wrong initial turns for these larger items and would require subsequent corrections that cost precious time and might mean losing some of the advantage over the competitors.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference.

claim: The flexibility found and the ability to operate on at least two types of prey that fall according to two different rules would allow at least some individual archerfish to efficiently handle two types of prey that co-occur during a specific time of the year.
source: The flexibility we found and the ability to operate on at least two types of prey that fall according to two different rules would allow at least some individual archerfish to efficiently handle two types of prey that co-occur during a specific time of the year.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: The ecological constraints and the severe competition that archerfish face in the wild could have favored the evolution of a decision that has the potential for plasticity and for combining speed, accuracy, and flexibility.
source: So, we suggest, clearly without proof, that the ecological constraints and the severe competition that archerfish face in the wild could have favored the evolution of a decision that has the potential for plasticity and for combining speed, accuracy, and flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: The findings demonstrate that highspeed decisions that lack a speed-accuracy tradeoff can offer learning capacities and cognitive aspects of much slower decisions and behaviors.
source: Our findings demonstrate that highspeed decisions that lack a speed-accuracy tradeoff are not necessarily limited to operating based on simplifying heuristics but can, at least in principle, offer learning capacities and cognitive aspects of much slower decisions and behaviors that occur at least at 100 times lesser speed.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: It will be exciting to see if the capacities found in archerfish are special or perhaps much more widespread among other highspeed decisions.
source: First, it will be exciting to see if the capacities we found in archerfish are special or perhaps much more widespread among other highspeed decisions.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction in the Discussion.

claim: If highspeed decisions are not generally incapable of learning and flexibility, the question remains more pressing what might be the other reasons that most decisions do show clear speed-accuracy trade-offs.
source: Second, if highspeed decisions are not generally incapable of learning and flexibility, the obvious question remains more pressing what might be the other reasons that most decisions do show clear speed-accuracy trade-offs (Chittka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a future direction in the Discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The findings suggest that rapid decision-making can be efficiently used in many technological applications in which time is premium – even if such applications require a high degree of flexibility.
source: Third, the findings suggest that rapid decision-making can be efficiently used in many technological applications in which time is premium – even if such applications require a high degree of flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application in the Discussion.

claim: Experiments were conducted on a group of six adult archerfish (Toxotes chatareus).
source: Experiments were conducted on a group of six adult archerfish (Toxotes chatareus).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: The experimental fish were randomly chosen from a larger group of archerfish.
source: The experimental fish were randomly chosen from a larger group of (male and female) archerfish.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: The fish had been imported from Thailand and were kept at 26 °C on a 12 hr:12 hr light/dark cycle.
source: They had been imported from Thailand (Aquarium Glaser, Rodgau, Germany) and were kept at 26 °C on a 12 hr:12 hr light/dark cycle in the large experimental tank (1 m × 1 m × 0.6 m, filled to a height of 34 cm) in brackish water (3.5 mS cm–1).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: All procedures were conducted in accordance with the German Animal Welfare Act and were approved by the government of Lower Franconia.
source: All procedures were conducted in accordance with the German Animal Welfare Act (Tierschutzgesetz) as well as the German Regulation for the protection of animals used for experimental purposes or other scientific purposes (Tierschutz-Versuchstierordnung) and were approved by the government of Lower Franconia (Regierung Unterfranken, Würzburg, Germany: Az. 2531-05-1).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: A 27'' LCD monitor (Samsung SyncMaster S27A750D, 120 fps, max. intensity 300 cd/m2) was used to present visual stimuli.
source: To present visual stimuli a 27'' LCD monitor (Samsung SyncMaster S27A750D, 120 fps, max. intensity 300 cd/m2) was used.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: All objects used in the study had a Michelson contrast of 0.96.
source: All objects used in this study had a Michelson contrast of 0.96, as determined with a luminance meter (LS-110 Konica Minolta Sensing Europe) under the conditions of the actual experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Objects that mimicked ballistically falling motion moved at a horizontal speed vh = 1.775 m s–1 and their virtual landing occurred 243 ms later, after a (virtual) path of 43 cm.
source: Objects that mimicked ballistically falling motion moved at a horizontal speed vh = 1.775 m s–1 and their virtual landing occurred 243 ms later, after a (virtual) path of 43 cm.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Objects on the 'deflected' trajectories moved at the same horizontal speed but changed the direction of motion after being visible for 116 ms by an angle ɣ=39.8° to the left.
source: Objects on the 'deflected' trajectories moved at the same horizontal speed but changed the direction of motion after being visible for 116 ms (or 20.5 cm) at a (virtual) time of 118.7 ms (i.e. after an initial straight path of dr = 21.1 cm) by an angle ɣ=39.8° to the left (see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Four feeders were typically present during experiments.
source: Unless stated otherwise, four feeders were typically present.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: All experiments on the start decisions require the competition within a group.
source: Because all experiments on the start decisions require the competition within a group (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008), we confirmed that all fish in the group always contributed to the decisions reported throughout the study.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with supporting citation.

claim: To ensure that the decisions could not be influenced by those of other fish, only the turn of the fish that responded first in each given test was analyzed.
source: To ensure that the decisions could not be influenced by those of other fish, we exclusively analyzed the turn of the fish that responded first in each given test.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Latency was the time between onset of movement of the prey object on the LED screen and the onset of the C-start.
source: Latency was the time between onset of movement of the prey object on the LED screen and the onset of the C-start.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: Error in aim relative to a point of interest was determined from the last frame at the end of the straightening phase (stage 2) of the C-start, before the fish starts its approach trajectory.
source: Error in aim relative to a point of interest (e.g. the virtual impact point) was determined from the last frame at the end of the straightening phase (stage 2) of the C-start, i.e., before the fish starts its approach trajectory (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.
